summary.text: The proof couples the mass-\(n+1\) evolution to the mass-\(n\) evolution by tracking the single extra unit: after each step its position advances exactly when the current cell is odd, and an invariant keeps it within two places of the leading block of unit cells. Thus stabilization for mass \(n\) forces stabilization for mass \(n+1\) within two further steps, while a reverse coupling and the characterization of a configuration one step before stability (either already stable or \(1^k2\)) show that the two first stabilization times cannot coincide.

full_proof.text:
We use positions numbered from 0. A configuration is a finite list
\[
c=(c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_{L-1})
\]
of positive integers. Its update is obtained by retaining \(\lceil c_i/2\rceil\) at position \(i\) and sending \(\lfloor c_i/2\rfloor\) to position \(i+1\). Thus, before a possible terminal zero is removed, the updated entries are
\[
 (Tc)_0=\left\lceil\frac{c_0}{2}\right\rceil,
 \qquad
 (Tc)_i=\left\lfloor\frac{c_{i-1}}2\right\rfloor+
          \left\lceil\frac{c_i}2\right\rceil \quad(1\le i<L),
\]
and
\[
 (Tc)_L=\left\lfloor\frac{c_{L-1}}2\right\rfloor.
\]
The last entry is omitted if it is zero.

It is useful to describe this operation recursively. Given an incoming carry \(r\geq 0\), define
\[
 F(r,[]) =
 \begin{cases}
 []&r=0,\\
 [r]&r>0,
 \end{cases}
\]
and
\[
 F(r,x::d)=\left(r+\left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil\right)::F\left(\left\lfloor\frac{x}{2}\right\rfloor,d\right).
\]
Then \(Tc=F(0,c)\). If every entry of \(c\) is positive, this recursive formula agrees exactly with the original update followed by deletion of trailing zeros. Indeed, every displayed nonterminal output
\(r+\lceil x/2\rceil\) is positive, and the only possible zero is the final carry. It also follows at once, by induction down the list, that \(Tc\) again has only positive entries and that its length is at least the length of \(c\).

For \(n\geq1\), let
\[
 C_n(t)=T^t([n])
\]
be the state after \(t\) updates, and write \(\mathbf 1_n\) for the list of \(n\) ones. Let
\[
 A(n)=\min\{t:C_n(t)=\mathbf 1_n\},
\]
once existence has been established below. The desired sequence value is exactly \(A(n)\), because the recursive update \(T\) is the cellular-automaton update just described.

The main idea is to couple the evolutions from masses \(n\) and \(n+1\).

For a list \(c\) and an index \(p\leq |c|\), let \(E_p(c)\) be the result of adding one unit at position \(p\): if \(p<|c|\), increase \(c_p\) by one, while if \(p=|c|\), append a new entry 1. We regard the value of \(c\) at the appended position as the virtual value 0. Define
\[
 \nu(c,p)=p+
 \begin{cases}
 1,&c_p\text{ is odd},\\
 0,&c_p\text{ is even},
 \end{cases}
\]
where the virtual value at \(p=|c|\) is 0 and hence even.

We first record the fundamental one-unit propagation identity
\[
 T(E_p(c))=E_{\nu(c,p)}(Tc). \tag{1}
\]
To prove it, process the list from left to right using \(F\). Until position \(p\), the two computations coincide. At position \(p\), use the elementary parity identities. If \(m\) is even, then
\[
 \left\lceil\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rceil=
 \left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil+1,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rfloor=
 \left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor;
\]
thus the extra unit remains at the current output position. If \(m\) is odd, then
\[
 \left\lceil\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rceil=
 \left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rfloor=
 \left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor+1;
\]
thus the extra unit becomes an additional incoming carry for the next position. Increasing an incoming carry by one increases the first subsequent output by one and changes nothing thereafter. This proves (1), including the case \(p=|c|\).

We now track where this extra unit can be. Let \(q(c)\) be the number of initial entries of \(c\) equal to 1. In other words, \(q(c)\) is the length of the initial block of ones. We say that a pair \((c,p)\) is good if
\[
 p\leq |c|, \tag{2}
\]
\[
 q(c)\leq p+2, \tag{3}
\]
and, if the first entry after the initial block of ones is 2, then
\[
 q(c)\leq p+1. \tag{4}
\]
When \(c\) consists entirely of ones, the entry mentioned in (4) does not exist, so (4) imposes no condition.

We need the following invariant.

**Invariant lemma.** If \(c\) has positive entries and \((c,p)\) is good, then \((Tc,\nu(c,p))\) is good.

Here is a proof, including the local cases behind the assertion. The length condition follows from \(p\leq |c|\), from \(\nu(c,p)\in\{p,p+1\}\), and from the fact that \(T\) does not shorten a positive list. More precisely, if \(p=|c|\), the virtual value is even and \(\nu=p\); if \(p<|c|\) and \(\nu=p+1\), the updated list has length at least \(|c|\geq p+1\).

For the two conditions involving the initial ones, induct on the list and distinguish whether \(p=0\) or \(p>0\). Write \(c=x::d\).

If \(p>0\) and \(x=1\), the first updated entry is again 1, and after removing this common first entry the assertion is exactly the same assertion for \(d\) and \(p-1\). Both the initial-one count and the tracked position have been decreased by one, so (3) and (4) translate exactly. This is the inductive case.

If \(p>0\) and \(x\ne1\), then the initial-one count of \(c\) is zero. In the updated list, the first entry is \(\lceil x/2\rceil\). If \(x\ge3\), either this entry is already not 1, or the only borderline values are handled directly by \(\lceil x/2\rceil\ge2\); hence the updated initial-one count is zero. If \(x=2\), the first output is 1, but the next output, when a next input exists, includes incoming carry 1 and is therefore at least 2; if there is no next input, the terminal carry itself is 1. In all cases there can be at most the small initial block required by (3), while \(\nu(c,p)\ge1\). If the first non-one is 2, (4) is also immediate because its initial-one count is at most the tracked position plus one. This proves this branch.

It remains to check \(p=0\). Here (3) says that \(c\) starts with at most two ones, and (4) rules out a 2 immediately after two initial ones.

* If \(x\ge3\), the first updated entry \(\lceil x/2\rceil\) is at least 2. Thus the updated initial-one count is zero, and both required inequalities are immediate, whether \(x\) is odd (so the new tracked position is 1) or even (so it is 0).

* If \(x=2\), the new tracked position remains 0. The first output is 1. If \(d\) is nonempty, its first output receives carry 1 and hence is at least 2, so the new initial-one count is 1; if \(d=[]\), then \(T[2]=[1,1]\), whose initial-one count is 2. Thus (3) holds. In the nonempty case, if the next entry is 2 then its position is 1, so the strengthened bound (4), namely \(1\le0+1\), holds; in the empty case there is no first non-one.

* If \(x=1\), the new tracked position is 1 and the first output is 1. Since the original list has at most two initial ones, the tail either begins with a non-one, begins with one followed by the end, or begins with one followed by an entry at least 3. The last assertion uses (4): an entry 2 after the two initial ones would violate \(2\le0+1\). If the tail begins with a value \(y\ne1\), then for \(y=2\) its updated contribution can create at most two further initial ones, while for \(y\ge3\) it immediately gives an output at least 2. If the tail begins with one, there are exactly two leading unchanged ones, and the next value, if any, is at least 3 and therefore stops the initial block after the update. Consequently the updated initial-one count is at most 3, which is (3) because the new position is 1. Moreover, whenever the first non-one output is 2, it occurs after at most two initial ones, giving (4), namely \(q(Tc)\le2=1+1\).

These cases prove the invariant lemma.

Define tracked positions \(P_n(t)\) recursively by
\[
 P_n(0)=0,
 \qquad
 P_n(t+1)=\nu(C_n(t),P_n(t)). \tag{5}
\]
The initial pair \(([n],0)\) is good: its initial-one count is 1 if \(n=1\), and 0 otherwise. By the invariant lemma, every pair
\[
 (C_n(t),P_n(t)) \tag{6}
\]
is good.

Equation (1) now gives, by induction on \(t\), the coupling identity
\[
 C_{n+1}(t)=E_{P_n(t)}(C_n(t)) \qquad(n\ge1). \tag{7}
\]
It is true at time 0 because \([n+1]=E_0([n])\). If it is true at time \(t\), apply \(T\), use (1), and then use recurrence (5).

We next derive a two-step upper bound on stabilization times. Suppose
\[
 C_n(t)=\mathbf1_n.
\]
For an all-ones list, \(q(\mathbf1_n)=n\). Goodness of \((\mathbf1_n,P_n(t))\) gives
\[
 P_n(t)\le n,\qquad n\le P_n(t)+2.
\]
Hence
\[
 P_n(t)\in\{n,n-1,n-2\}, \tag{8}
\]
with impossible negative cases simply absent for small \(n\).

By (7), the state of the \((n+1)\)-system at time \(t\) is obtained by adding one unit at one of these three positions. The three possibilities can be computed explicitly.

1. If \(P_n(t)=n\), then
\[
E_n(\mathbf1_n)=\mathbf1_{n+1},
\]
which remains fixed under every further update.

2. If \(P_n(t)=n-1\), then
\[
E_{n-1}(\mathbf1_n)=\mathbf1_{n-1}\mathbin{++}[2].
\]
One update sends the final 2 to two ones, so
\[
T(\mathbf1_{n-1}\mathbin{++}[2])=\mathbf1_{n+1}.
\]

3. If \(P_n(t)=n-2\), then
\[
E_{n-2}(\mathbf1_n)=\mathbf1_{n-2}\mathbin{++}[2,1].
\]
The first update gives
\[
T(\mathbf1_{n-2}\mathbin{++}[2,1])
 =\mathbf1_{n-1}\mathbin{++}[2],
\]
and the second gives \(\mathbf1_{n+1}\).

Thus, in every case,
\[
 C_{n+1}(t+2)=\mathbf1_{n+1}. \tag{9}
\]
(The all-ones configuration is fixed, so this remains true even in the cases that stabilize earlier.)

This also proves that stabilization always occurs. For \(n=1\), \(C_1(0)=[1]\). If the mass-\(n\) system stabilizes at some time \(t\), (9) says that the mass-\((n+1)\) system stabilizes by time \(t+2\). Induction on \(n\) therefore establishes the existence of \(A(n)\) for every \(n\ge1\). Applying (9) at \(t=A(n)\) gives
\[
 A(n+1)\le A(n)+2. \tag{10}
\]

It remains to prove the strict lower bound
\[
 A(n+1)>A(n). \tag{11}
\]
Several elementary reverse implications are needed.

First, if \(c\) has positive entries, \(p\le|c|\), and
\[
 E_p(c)=\mathbf1_{N+1},

a direct induction from the left shows that
\[
 c=\mathbf1_N. \tag{12}
\]
Indeed, adding at position 0 to a nonempty positive list makes its first entry at least 2, so it cannot produce an all-ones list. If \(p>0\), the first entry is unchanged and therefore must be 1; remove it and apply the same argument to the tail and position \(p-1\). The empty-list endpoint is immediate. Combining (12) with (7), we obtain
\[
 C_{n+1}(k)=\mathbf1_{n+1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_n(k)=\mathbf1_n. \tag{13}
\]
Consequently \(A(n)\le A(n+1)\). To make this inequality strict, we show that the \((n+1)\)-system is not stable at time \(A(n)\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that both systems are stable then. Equation (7) gives
\[
 E_{P_n(A(n))}(\mathbf1_n)=\mathbf1_{n+1}.
\]
Adding a unit to an all-ones list can leave an all-ones list only by appending at its end. Hence
\[
 P_n(A(n))=n. \tag{14}
\]
For \(n=1\), this is already impossible: \(A(1)=0\), while \(P_1(0)=0\), not 1.

Assume now \(n\ge2\). Since \([n]\ne\mathbf1_n\), we have \(A(n)>0\). Put
\[
 u=A(n)-1.
\]
Then \(C_n(u)\) is not stable, but its next update is \(\mathbf1_n\). We classify all positive predecessors of an all-ones list:
\[
 Tc=\mathbf1_N
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c=\mathbf1_N
\quad\text{or}\quad
\bigl(N=k+2\text{ and }c=\mathbf1_k\mathbin{++}[2]\bigr). \tag{15}
\]

To prove (15), write \(c=x::d\). Since the first output is \(\lceil x/2\rceil=1\) and \(x>0\), one has \(x=1\) or \(x=2\). If \(x=1\), no positive carry enters the tail, so apply the same argument inductively to \(d\): either the tail is all ones, or it is some ones followed by one final 2. If \(x=2\), the tail is processed with incoming carry 1. If the tail were nonempty, its first output would be
\[
1+\left\lceil\frac y2\right\rceil\ge2,
\]
contrary to the all-ones output. Thus the tail is empty; the incoming carry supplies the second output 1, and \([2]\) maps to \([1,1]\). This is exactly the second alternative with \(k=0\). This proves (15).

The first alternative in (15) is impossible for \(c=C_n(u)\), because it would mean that the mass-\(n\) system stabilized at the earlier time \(u<A(n)\). Therefore, writing \(n=k+2\),
\[
 C_n(u)=\mathbf1_k\mathbin{++}[2]. \tag{16}
\]
Here \(k=n-2\).

We now use the strengthened part (4) of the positional invariant. If \((\mathbf1_k\mathbin{++}[2],p)\) is good, then its initial-one count is \(k\), its length is \(k+1\), and the first non-one is 2. Therefore
\[
 p\le k+1,
 \qquad
 k\le p+1. \tag{17}
\]
Thus \(p\) is one of \(k-1,k,k+1\), omitting impossible negative values. We claim that
\[
 \nu(\mathbf1_k\mathbin{++}[2],p)\ne k+2. \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, if \(p=k+1\), the entry there is 2, which is even, so \(\nu=p=k+1\). If \(p=k\), the entry is 2 and again \(\nu=k\). If \(p=k-1\), the entry is 1, so \(\nu=k\). This proves (18).

Apply this with \(p=P_n(u)\), which is good by (6), and use (16). Recurrence (5) says
\[
P_n(A(n))=P_n(u+1)
 =\nu(C_n(u),P_n(u))
e k+2=n.
\]
This contradicts (14). We have proved
\[
 C_{n+1}(A(n))\ne\mathbf1_{n+1}. \tag{19}
\]

Now (13), applied at time \(A(n+1)\), gives \(A(n)\le A(n+1)\). Equality would contradict (19), because the mass-\((n+1)\) system is stable at its defining time \(A(n+1)\). Hence (11) follows:
\[
 A(n)<A(n+1).
\]
Combining this strict inequality with (10), and using integrality, leaves exactly two possibilities:
\[
 A(n+1)=A(n)+1
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 A(n+1)=A(n)+2.
\]
Finally, \(A(n)\) is precisely the number \(a(n)\) of cellular-automaton steps required to reach \(n\) unit cells, because \(T\) is the stated simultaneous halving-and-transfer rule and its recursive representation differs only by omitting the possible terminal zero. Therefore, for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
 a(n+1)-a(n)\in\{1,2\},
\]
as required.
